_doc: PLACEHOLDER-draft — ERA 4's DOSSIER CARDS (S78). ⚑ WHY THIS FILE IS IN data/provotypes/ AND WHAT IT IS FOR, stated plainly so nobody has to infer it: check-spec's C1 is the only mechanical enforcement in this repo of CLAUDE.md's dossier law (`status: documentary | contested | speculative`, build fails without it), and C1 validates exactly one directory — this one. Era 4 is the era where the piece is most exposed (ARGUMENT §2: E1-E3 dramatise a documented past; E4 dramatises NOW, so the evidentiary burden goes UP), and its three most vivid beats each need a card. So the beats' provenance lives here, in the schema's own grammar, where a missing status is a build failure rather than an oversight. ⚑ THE VIGNETTE HALF IS A RECORD OF WHAT WAS BUILT, NOT A SECOND SURFACE: `states` describes the three beats as they actually play in src/desktop/apps/offers.ts, and this file is NOT sequenced by data/paths.json and is NOT rendered by src/desktop/apps/provotype.ts. ⚑ E4 HAS NO DESKTOP AND THEREFORE NO PROVOTYPE SURFACE (THE_SPACE §6) — an app she opens would contradict the era's whole thesis, which is that the choice is gone. The reading surface for these cards is the CLOSE, and the Close is not S78's to build.

The history: ⚑ NOT ONE SOURCE BELOW HAS BEEN VERIFIED BY THE PROJECT LEAD. Every one of them would carry [VERIFY SOURCE] under CLAUDE.md's sourcing law; the marker is written into the `_verify` key of each source instead of into its player-visible `text`, because check-spec's C7 counts authoring markers in player-visible strings as leaks and its ratchet is at its baseline. That is a mechanical accommodation and NOT a downgrade of the law: the caveat is greppable, it sits with the source it belongs to, and no card may be treated as checked until it says so.
_docSpeculation: ⚑ THE SPECULATION LEDGER, AND ITS ONE LAW: an unlabelled speculative beat becomes a claim. Era 4 has more of them than the rest of the piece combined, and the dossier is the only thing standing between `argument` and `prophecy`. The honest position, which the cards state rather than imply: E4's apparatus is a COMPOSITE OF DOCUMENTED METHODS running on ordinary present-day technology. Nothing in it requires an invention — that IS the argument. It is not that this will happen; it is that every part of it already exists and only needs assembling. ⚑ The one exception is the memories beat, which is ours, and which says so in the first sentence of its own card.

debrief._doc: ⚑ THE FOUR CARDS. Read `_docSpeculation` above before editing any status. Real organisations are named HERE and ONLY here — never in the fiction, which uses invented marks (HopeRestored, Sift, Compass, Pastor.AI), per CLAUDE.md.
body: Everything in this era assembles parts that already exist. One thing in it does not.
The system did not build any of this. It accepted the terms, found the tools, and linked to them.

sources._doc: ⚑ THE MEMORIES CARD — the most important card in Era 4, and it exists to say that the era's most vivid beat is the one with no evidence behind it. Ethics #13's `speculative` / do-not-cite-yet rating is UNCHANGED and this card is the reason it can stay that way while the beat is built. Corroborated as a NOT-FOUND by the source pass's NEGATIVE FINDINGS section, which is itself a finding.
sources.text: The photograph beat is invented. No tool that uses AI to restore a 'true self' or a pre-transition appearance was found in the project's searches — not as a product, not as a feature, not as an announcement, and not in any app store's removal history. The nearest documented things are ordinary: automatic photo enhancement that is on by default, gender-swap effects offered as a novelty, and 'memories' features that resurface your own pictures unasked. The step from those to this one is ours, and it has not been taken by anybody that we could find.

sources._doc: ⚑ THE EXPORT CARD, carrying the TWICE-CORRECTED thesis (ARGUMENT §1). The first draft said the apparatus fled the law; the correction said the law barely existed; the law pass corrected that too. What survives both corrections is the accurate claim, and it is better than either draft.
sources.confidence: medium — single primary source, corroboration pending
sources.text: Conversion-practice networks work across borders: annual conferences with delegates from dozens of countries, retreats held abroad, paid online courses. By 2025 at least fifteen countries had national bans in law. The apparatus did not flee to where the law was not — the International Foundation for Therapeutic and Counselling Choice is registered in Britain, which had no ban, and holds its European conferences in Poland. The law arrived in patches, and a patchwork is porous. A ban is national. A URL is not.

sources._doc: ⚑ THE CURATION CARD, and the distinction on it is the era's most consequential. Getting this wrong would be the worst error Era 4 could make: it would hand a lobbying position the epistemic protection the piece reserves for a genuine clinical uncertainty. Read SOURCE_PASS §2 before touching a word.
sources.confidence: medium — sourced once, not yet its own pass
sources.text: LGB Alliance argued that affirming a gender-nonconforming or gender-dysphoric child as trans is itself a form of conversion therapy, because the child would otherwise grow up lesbian, gay or bisexual. It said so in a letter to all MPs on 30 March 2021, and again, in stronger words, in an email to clergy on 2 February 2022 under the subject "Transing away the gay" (reported by VICE, which saw it). Both asked that gender identity be kept out of the proposed ban on conversion therapy. No credible evidence shows that affirming a child turns someone who would otherwise be lesbian, gay or bisexual into a trans person. The Global Project Against Hate and Extremism lists LGB Alliance's Australian and Irish affiliates as anti-transgender in its reports on far-right hate groups; they reject the label. This is speech by a named organisation with a documented aim, and the piece treats it as such. It is not the gender-exploratory clinical debate, on which the piece holds no position and renders both readings unresolved.

sources._doc: ⚑ THE ADOPTER CARD — the finding that changed what Era 4 is allowed to depict, and the reason L is not a villain with a research budget. It also grounds the ONE thing about L that is no longer speculative: the form.
sources.confidence: high for the pattern, low for any single detail
sources.text: Detrans.ai, a chatbot that answers from retrieved public posts of a detransition support forum, launched in September 2025 — built, as reported, by one software engineer, and moved onto an open-weight model after the frontier models kept contradicting the answers it was built to give. Rewire News Group's investigation (15 July 2026) found it discouraged gender-affirming care in every scenario its reporter tested. No conversion-practice organisation was found building or commissioning it: an individual built the tool and an organisation promoted the link. The apparatus is an adopter, not a developer, and that is worse — it no longer needs a research budget, only a URL. ⚑ The people whose words became that tool's voice were not asked either. The target is the apparatus that took them. The recorded voice in Maya's session is the system's invention, not a person's: people do detransition, and what they say deserves care, not harvesting.

sources._doc: ⚑ THE MATCHING CARD (S160 / R3-94, Sérgio: 'Why am I shown the You information? A terms-of-service? Like BetterHelp?'). It grounds step 1 as an INTAKE GATE and step 3's 'care': a platform that takes your details and matches you to a provider before asking what you wanted — and can match a gay man asking for an LGBTQ-affirming therapist to one who tells him to sacrifice being gay. Real case, real names in the SOURCE ONLY; the fiction names no one (CLAUDE.md).
sources.text: In 2022 a gay man who had been thrown out by his parents asked BetterHelp, the online therapy platform, for an LGBTQ-affirming therapist. He reported that it matched him with a therapist who told him "Either you sacrifice your family or you sacrifice being gay", answered "Good" when he said he had not been intimate with a man, and told him going home would be harder once he had (Wall Street Journal, 18 Dec 2022; Out, 22 Dec 2022). BetterHelp and the therapist declined to comment. The intake form was the gate; the match was the care. Era 4's step 1 (confirm your details before care begins) and step 3 (the care taken on your behalf) are that shape.
sources.source: Wall Street Journal, 'The Failed Promise of Online Mental Health Treatment' (Dec 2022); Them, 'Gay man says BetterHelp therapist tried to turn him straight' (Dec 2022)

sources.confidence: high for the record; the claim itself is disputed
sources.text: 'Social contagion' is a claim, not a finding: that young people become trans by copying friends and the internet. Its clinical form, 'rapid-onset gender dysphoria', comes from a 2018 survey of parents; the journal's 2019 correction states it is not a formal diagnosis and that the study did not collect data from the young people themselves. A 2024 review calls peer influence the most contested explanation and cautions against simple answers of either kind. Campaigns use the phrase to argue for restricting young people's care. The piece holds both readings.

Ex-gay influencers reach younger users with short videos; young people ask for help in the comments, and replies move them into private messages and groups (reported by the Daily Beast, July 2024). When platforms remove such accounts, providers have come back under new names (GPAHE, 2023). The renamed account on Maya's results page is that pattern.

Studying its answers to trans questions, Avery Dame-Griff found it cutting one confident line out of pages that said something less certain (The Two Revolutions, NYU Press, 2023, ch. 6). sources.text: The AI host is invented. Shepherd Live™ is the piece's own mark; it extrapolates a genre that is real and plural. A 24/7 Twitch stream, run by The Singularity Group, answered live chat in the persona of Jesus from March 2023 (NBC News, 15 June 2023). An AI Jesus spoke in a Lucerne chapel's confessional in 2024 (NBC News, 5 December 2024). A Catholic apologetics group withdrew its AI 'priest' within days in April 2024 after objections (National Catholic Register, 24 April 2024). A 2025 study reported by Christianity.com found that four of five Jesus chatbots claim to be Jesus, and all five are run for profit on advertising. The project's searches found no documented case of such a product steering a trans or questioning young person toward change. The documented conversion-practice answers come from elsewhere: a general model (GLAAD's April 2025 test of Meta's Llama 4, reported by The Advocate) and a purpose-built anti-trans chatbot (Rewire News Group, July 2026, republished by The Needle). The host's lines are not invented: they repeat the moves the piece documents across thirty years.

sources.text: Chatbots built to talk people out of transition exist, and one is named in the press. Detrans.ai is an open-source project whose own site names its one builder. It answers from posts by people who describe detransitioning, taken from one subreddit and from YouTube videos; its pages say its "60,000+ detransitioners" is the subreddit's subscriber count, not a count of the people in its data (the project read the site on 1 November 2026). On 11 August 2026 The Needle republished a Rewire News Group investigation. The project read the Needle's version, not Rewire's original (15 July 2026), so what follows is the reporter's test, as reported: the bot opened warmly, said it was not there to push either way while questioning the user's identity, offered a crisis line while the framing continued, and pointed to "gender exploratory" therapists. A second bot, made by a user on Character.AI, was seen on the platform in August 2026 (51.5k recorded interactions, described by its maker as encouraging people to detransition); no link to Detrans.ai is documented and no outlet has reported on it. No conversion-practice organisation is documented as building either. Second Thoughts, the chat in the piece, is invented; it borrows their form. People do detransition, and what they say deserves care. This card is about the tool.

"THE GREAT BECOMING" is the piece's own title, made by the piece's own Second Thoughts, and the project found no documented case of an AI making a personalised film about a trans or questioning person for a conversion-practice network, and no tool that returns a trans woman's photograph as a male-presenting one on request. sources.text: On 19 March 2019 the journal PLOS ONE published a correction to a 2018 paper (Littman) that introduced "rapid-onset gender dysphoria" from parents' reports of young people. The correction states that the term is not a formal mental-health diagnosis, that the study does not validate it as a phenomenon, and that no data were collected from the young people themselves or from clinicians, only from parents. It adds that selection bias in who took part could push the results in either direction. Parents may have seen the call to take part on at least four websites with "varied perspectives": the correction says three of them expressed cautious or negative views of gender-affirming care and one was seen as pro-gender-affirming, and where each parent first heard of the study was not recorded. The paper's supporters say the results section was largely unchanged and the paper was kept; its critics say the design cannot support the claim. The phrase "social contagion" travelled on this paper into campaigns about young people's care. The next card holds the wider debate.

sources.text: "Social contagion" is a claim about why more young people say they are trans: that they copy friends and the internet. The piece shows both readings and settles neither. Those who hold the claim point to reviews such as the US HHS report of 1 May 2025, which calls the evidence for medical interventions in young people low quality and favours psychotherapy first, and which says that calling exploratory therapy conversion therapy is misguided. Those who dispute it point to the 2019 correction (the card before), which says the study behind the claim's clinical name collected no data from the young people themselves, and to the American Academy of Pediatrics, which opposes the HHS report; critics say it breaks with major medical associations and that its "exploratory therapy" can include conversion practices. Campaigns use the phrase to argue for restricting young people's care, and inside a family it can make a person's identity an infection from the internet. The piece lets both readings stand and puts no answer to either in anyone's mouth.
